Miranda Davies writes

The controversial element that Lanyado offers for discussion is the use of the therapist's personality in the ‘present relationship’. She presents it from the vantage point of a psychoanalytic tradition that works strictly in the transference relationship and shows from her clinical experience that there are times when the patient needs the therapist to respond authentically, through actions, from her self. This is seen as a move in a new direction.

For Jungians in the ‘London School’ the move over the last fifty years has been in the opposite direction. Jung was very much against the rigid and unintegrated use of theory and emphasized the quality of the analyst's personality as an essential factor in healing; he associated healing with compassion, an element that has more recently been linked with the therapist's warmth, genuineness and empathy. Jung's objection was not to the need for reserve in psychoanalysis, but to an idealization that resulted in too rigid an application.

In this regard necessity is indeed the mother of invention, for the analyst must constantly strive to develop his techniques in such a way that they can be of help even in the most difficult cases. We owe it to the difficulties presented by the daily treatment of the sick that we were driven to formulate views which shake the foundations of our everyday beliefs.

(Jung 1948: 270)

In his writing he showed repeated concern that the application of a theory should not override the patient's individuality.

This book is a collection of papers on adolescence written by senior psychoanalytic psychotherapists from various European countries. The varied contributions are held together powerfully by a common thread: adolescence is a unique developmental stage in which it is still possible to re-elaborate deep conflicts experienced in childhood. Coming from different theoretical backgrounds and from different clinical practices the authors share the belief that, as well as being a period of great vulnerability, adolescence also possesses great resources in the ability to reconstruct and compensate. As Anastasopoulos says in his foreword, ‘adolescence contains components that are capable of leading either to the restoration of the fragmented personality or to a hell in which chaotic disturbance can be permanent’.

For the therapist, the possibility of a second chance, of modifying the adolescent's internal world and consequently their future, can be both exciting and overwhelming. There is a potential for therapists to experience at once omnipotent and completely hopeless feelings which belong in large measure to the adolescent's extreme and confused state of mind.

A recurrent theme throughout is the quality of continuous thought needed to help those adolescents whose essential mental equipment is faulty to face the challenge of growing up. The struggle to reach the adolescent patient in order to avoid the ever-present possibility of psychic breakdown or of dangerous acting out, and the need to maintain a balanced closeness/distance in the therapeutic relationship, are underlined by all the authors. The continuous search for ‘the right technique’ demonstrates both the uncertainties and worries as well as the dedication and the challenges faced by therapists. Great importance is given to both the function and the use of interpretation, with some authors stressing that the therapist's first aim is to stand in as a supplementary ego, particularly in those cases where the adolescent has suffered from childhood traumas, which are often re-enacted in adolescence in a state of confusion or dissociation. As Anastasopoulos says in his paper ‘The influence of psychic traumas’, if it is essential to recognize the external trauma, it is equally important not to reinforce the defences around the patient's fantasies by dealing excessively with the dramatic nature of the external event, which might lead to repeating that abusive and traumatic situation in the transference relationship. The author is very attuned to the therapists’ vulnerability when faced with such traumatic events which seem to completely fill the mental and emotional space leaving no room for thinking and for working through.

Alphabetical list of contributors: Anne Alvarez, Francis Dale, Susanna Isaacs Elmhirst, Renata Gaddini, James Grotstein, Genevieve Haag, Victoria Hamilton, Didier Houzel, Jo-Ann Culbert-Koehn, Bianca Lechevalier, Suzanne Maiello, Judith Mitrani, Theodore Mitrani, Thomas Ogden, Maria Pozzi, Maria Rhode, Charlotte Riley, David Rosenfeld, Sheila Spensley, Jane van Buren, Isca Wittenberg.

‘You do not need to be limited by your lecturers, teachers, analysts, parents. If you are, then there is no room for growth’ (Bion, 1980) Frances Tustin quoted this maxim of Bion's in her description of her analysis with him, and she acknowledged how these thoughts gave her the courage to think for herself and progress beyond the comfort zone of currently accepted views when the results of her own clinical experience led her forward into new theoretical areas.

This collection brings together the words and the thoughts of an international collection of analytic workers who found themselves profoundly influenced by this lively and unsentimental woman. It is a book rich in powerful clinical vignettes from work both with children and adults: work which continually blazes the trail for thinking to be modified and extended in the intellectually rigorous way that Frances Tustin herself exemplified: ‘Our loyalty should be to understanding rather than personalities.’

And yet, perhaps paradoxically, it was indeed the powerful impression of her personality which inspired those who came after her to ‘go beyond’, as Suzanne Maiello describes in her eponymous chapter which opens the book in fine style, linking Tustin's thinking to her own continuing researches (Maiello, 2000) into the possible prenatal roots of primitive mental states. Such work is beginning to answer Bion's question when he wondered ‘when psychoanalysis would catch up with the foetus’ (Bion, 1978).

Space does not permit me to do justice to the full content of each chapter. Contributors have been led to extend what they received and make it their own in a truly Bionic sense. Reading their reference lists in itself opens up new areas to explore. A brief outline of each chapter's contents will, I hope, be enough to guide readers on their own journey through the book.

I confess to having been unfamiliar with the concept of ‘communicative psychoanalysis’ before reading this book, and I imagine this may be the case with other child psychotherapists in Britain and elsewhere, as it is a theoretical framework not frequently cited in papers published in this Journal or others especially known to our profession. The author is Canadian and received training from Robert Langs, who together with another American, Harold Searles, has been responsible for developments in this field since the 1960s. There are now International and European Societies for Communicative Psychoanalysis, and a journal published from New York.

I think this is a book which could arouse a range of thoughts and emotions in child psychotherapists. It seems almost infuriatingly didactic and prescriptive at times; it sometimes adopts a not altogether attractive polemical tone - for example, when fulminating against the perceived hostility of the American psychoanalytical establishment towards the ideas of communicative psychoanalysts (though it then, it is hinted, adopted some of them without due acknowledgement). At times it seems to veer away from the main theme to explore philosophical issues such as freedom to play. Nevertheless, there are some thought-provoking ideas, raising questions of theory and technique, on which I have found it useful to reflect. Indeed, what can be described as the central theme of the book is rather challenging and provocative: do we really communicate with our patients or do we ‘speculatively intervene’?

The book is divided into three sections: theory and technique, clinical material, and a third part entitled ‘Are we created equal?’ In the first section, Bonac develops the work done by Langs with adults on free association and the meaning ascribed by patients to the implications of the therapist's communications and actions. Bonac wishes to put this at the forefront of her thinking about work with children:

The course of therapy could be described as an interactional spiralling process: at each and every moment in a session, both participants of the therapeutic process respond consciously and unconsciously to the realities of a given situation and thus contribute to the ever changing process. When the therapist pays attention to the sequence and details of this interactional process the result is a truthful application of the concept of a two-person psychology in reality, not only in theory and belief.

This scholarly volume is by an Australian child analyst working within a Lacanian paradigm. The early history of child analysis is presented sympathetically in chapters on Freud and Little Hans, Hermine Hug-Hellmuth, Anna Freud, Melanie Klein and Winnicott. The second half of the book offers an account of Lacan's thinking about analysis with children and the clinical researches of some of his pupils.

Rodriguez's emphasis is on the child's capacity to engage as an active analysand -a ‘subject’ in Lacanian terminology - and his profound respect for the child's capacity for observation, questioning and thought is clearly signalled in his delightful exploration of ‘Little Hans’. Freud's relationship to the Graf family is well described, but the central focus is on Hans’ development as a speaker and questioner. This is one of the points of convergence with Kleinian conceptions, since Klein's ‘epistemophilic instinct’ has an obvious affinity to Lacan's concept of the ‘ethics of speaking well’, as the aim of psychoanalysis. ‘Speaking well’ is defined as the capacity for creative self-reflection and exploration through conversation within the analytic setting.

The chapters on the early practitioners of child analysis are appreciative in tone, while attempting to offer a critical perspective. Hug-Hellmuth's battered reputation is set in the context of her originality. Her observations of the impact of the transference on a child were an important starting point.

Peter Wilson  

The importance of this book is that it brings alive, once again, the extraordinary complexity of the hysteria that resides within more of us than most of us care to think. For many, hysteria may have lost its place in contemporary psychoanalytic preoccupation, consigned for the most part to memories of the tribulations of ladies of a certain type, now long gone. Considering, however, the ever-increasing waves of public hysteria that seem to awash our contemporary experience, this in some ways is surprising. Prevailing interest in borderline phenomena, the influence of infancy and attachment theory sit curiously in a world seemingly caught up in the fray of frenetic sexual display. Could it be that psychoanalysis has chosen, like the hysteric, to repress sexuality? As Christopher Bollas suggests in this fascinating book, ‘it is arguable that the rise of the borderline personality in the 1950s drawing psychoanalysts’ interests towards the “primitive” and the “pre-oedipal”, constituted an hysterical movement within the psychoanalytic community itself’.

Taking to heart Laplanche's protest against the ‘desexualization’ of psychoanalysis, Bollas has written a book that powerfully reminds us of the force of sexuality in personality development and of its vicissitudes in the many forms of hysteria. He builds substantially on Freud's Studies on Hysteria and takes us much further, not merely leaving us with a variation of the ordained view. Rather, he weaves a web of thought and ‘imaginary’ into a fresh level of theory that is inventive and elucidatory in helping us make sense of the subtlety of the hysterical personality.

The key issue in Bollas’ study is the hysteric's sheer inability to integrate the reality of the sexual body and in particular the genitals. He or she (for, unlike the traditional view, Bollas believes that hysteria resides equally within both genders) is at odds with the body. He or she is terrified of physical and mental intimacy. Sexuality is seen as essentially disruptive, an intrusive threat to the pre-Oedipal relationship with the mother and an unwelcome reminder of the presence of the father with the mother and as representative of an external order.

The chapters contained in this volume were all presented as papers at the event held in November 1996 at the Tavistock Clinic, in celebration of Donald Meltzer's 75th birthday. It was an uplifting event: Meltzer himself at the centre of a group of those keen to tell him of the clinical experiences and applications and thinking that they had developed from his writings and teachings. It must have been a painful task for the editors of this volume, Margaret Cohen and Alberto Hahn, to have to omit any of the papers presented to the conference. It seems that they made their choice to be as representative as possible: by topic, and by the nationality and gender of the presenter. What is clear from this volume is the richness of the work presented, and of the many different directions in which individuals have moved while acknowledging the inspiration of Meltzer for their work. What is particularly impressive is that the acknowledgement is made to him, and to his antecedent thinkers, with respect, but not with too much. These are people who are both indebted but independent in their thinking, and who in turn make their own contribution. That is probably the greatest accolade to Donald Meltzer.

The position described by Shirley Hoxter is perhaps central when she speaks of ‘my personal struggle of slowly learning how to learn from him’. His writing can be difficult. His meaning can be clear and then suddenly become obfuscated. He can be didactic without sufficient elucidation, very different from the Meltzer of the clinical master class in which the presenter is in the co-operative and sometimes humorous relationship with him that leads to memorable experiences of learning. I personally cannot speak of the experience of individual supervision. But I do know that it can be when in his writing he is at his most didactic, even irritating, that the new thought can surprise, the more creative moment can develop. His method is so different from the precisions of Bion; but also with Meltzer it is the reader who must do the work in order to reap the rewards. Meltzer can be a veritable gadfly; his sting produces the leap to that new thought.

Anyone with a first-hand knowledge of Anna Freud's psychoanalytic thinking, lucky enough to work at the Hampstead Child Therapy Course and Clinic1 during her directorship, would find it a forbidding task to give any overall account of her psychoanalytic thinking. This is largely, though not entirely, due to the remarkably wide range of her interests: normal and abnormal development from earliest infancy to old age; theory of technique and therapy; residential care; family structure and interactions within it; separation and bereavement; nursery schooling and education in general; delinquency; psychological effects of physical illness; developmental anomalies; childhood borderline states and psychosis of all kinds (including its manifestations in adults); family law - the list goes on and on.

There are other reasons for the difficulty, of which the most imponderable is the extent to which her achievements were linked to her personality. Its public aspect could be seen in her incisive thinking and seemingly simple eloquence at innumerable meetings and discussions, in her participation in the work of study groups, and in her chairmanship of meetings open to the wider psychoanalytic public. All of these supplemented and enlarged on her written work, and more than a few gave rise to it. But the system of study groups and specialized responsibilities meant that no one person could be present at more than a few of the clinic's many events. At a personal level, she would be best known for the close interest she took in the individual's professional activities, though personal circumstances and difficulties did not escape her. But these constructive involvements were those of an otherwise private person. Anna Freud was austere, admitting few intimates, but was many sided and had a seductive charm on which she drew to realize potentials in her staff that were not always known to their possessor. Deeply respected, everyone knew the same person, but each in a somewhat different way. In an account of her professional thinking, the interests the writer most closely shared with Anna Freud would have to be subordinate to a wider picture. Clearly, that daunting task calls for qualities beyond considerations of form and style.

Most of the contributors to this book are staff members of the Tavistock Clinic who are also teachers on the child psychotherapy training.

It may be worth noting the title, which uses the word ‘in’ rather than ‘for’. The implication is that assessment is here to be understood as a piece of work that can be an end in itself, ‘a brief intervention with therapeutic potential’. Much of the work described comes under the heading of ‘therapeutic consultation’, and the book is possibly partly aimed as a contribution to the place of brief work as one of the core skills of child psychotherapists - a major issue for child psychotherapy within the NHS.

While readers will find much in the book that informs them on questions and decisions to be made regarding longer-term individual therapy, the prevailing message is that assessment is neither an exact art nor a prescriptive process leading to exact conclusions. The general message regarding treatment following assessment is that psychotherapy is suitable for any responsive child where the family and network (including co-working therapists) support it. Frequency of sessions, with some important exceptions, is mainly left to a consideration of what can be managed, taking everything from consent and motivation to logistics into account.

Though readers will find a chapter on the under-5s (in a special context) and a section on adolescence, the format eschews a steady churning through the ages and stages of development, and of matters relevant to them. The word ‘latency’ will not be found anywhere, even once, and the word ‘puberty’ occurs, in passing, just twice.

The book is divided into four sections, the first two of which are about work with children with very severe psychopathology, while the last two are about family work and adolescence, respectively. There is considerable overlap between sections and between chapters.

Editorial

Paul Barrows and Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham  

In this edition of the journal we focus on the theme of trauma. In its many forms, child psychotherapists are increasingly having to work with the effects of trauma. Often this is not so much the impact of a single, major traumatic event so much as the cumulative impact of long-term abuse or neglect. In a recent paper in this journal, for example, Kenrick (2000) drew attention to the damaging effect of the repeated trauma of separation for looked-after children. In addition, we would emphasize, along with Perry et al. (1995), the traumatogenic impact of neglect: ‘Deprivation of critical experiences during development may be the most destructive yet least understood area of child maltreatment.’

In his opening paper Balbernie summarizes for us some of the most recent advances in our understanding of neuroscience, and particularly draws out the implications of this work for our appreciation of the devastating effects that trauma can have and the way these effects actually become wired into the very structure of the brain. This has major implications for us in terms of our thinking about therapeutic practice and Balbernie rightly underlines the value of early intervention.

With this in mind, Mohler et al.'s paper illustrates precisely this approach, as they describe a therapeutic intervention with an 8-week-old girl. Here we can see at first hand how the infant's presence can evoke the trans-generational re-enactment of traumas from the mother's own childhood which, as we know from the work of Main and Hesse (1990), can lead to states of disorganized attachment in the child.

Sadly, of course, such well-informed early interventions are often not available or there may be a variety of reasons why children fail to get help at this stage. Despite our increasing knowledge, it remains all too true that ‘It is an ultimate irony that at the time when the human is most vulnerable to the effects of trauma—during infancy and childhood—adults generally presume the most resilience’ (Perry, 1995). When help has not been available then children are likely to need the ‘second chance’—in Rustin's words—that therapy can provide. In the following three clinical papers by Rustin, Ralph and Youell each in their own way movingly illustrates the painstaking work—and emotional investment—required of the therapist to gradually unpick the damage.

Adrian Sutton

Adrian Sutton

195 Hathersage Road
Manchester M13 0JE

Adrian Sutton   Consultant in Child and Family Psychiatry and Psychotherapy at the Winnicott Centre, Manchester. He has a special interest in the application of psychoanalytic theory across the breadth of child and adolescent mental health, including its use in individual psychotherapy with children and concurrent working with their parents (or alternative carers). Involvement with research and the undergraduate and postgraduate education of doctors and other disciplines has led to cross-fertilization of ideas with educationalists and ethicists and an enhanced appreciation of the usefulness of psychoanalytic thinking in these arenas.
Autonomy, informed consent, child psychotherapy, resistance, therapeutic alliance,

There are inherent difficulties in reconciling concepts of ‘freedom of choice’, ‘autonomy’ and ‘informed consent’ with the idea of unconscious mechanisms. If mechanisms prevent issues being available to consciousness and the possibility of internal or interpersonal dialogue, then what or whom do we believe is giving or withholding consent? In addition to dynamic issues, consideration of maturational processes is essential when making judgements in this arena. There are increased expectations that children should be active participants in making decisions about their own health and welfare: further thought needs to be given to the implications of this for psychotherapy. This paper considers these issues specifically in relation to the latency phase. In therapy, we aim to assist a child in moving from a predominating or seriously distorting reliance on primitive mechanisms. However, before the latency child is sufficiently established in this we may also be faced with developmentally appropriate mechanisms which result in the submergence of experiences which may still be linked with pathological elements. Simultaneously, pathological and healthy processes may lead to resistance in therapy.

Using material from the therapy of a young boy who entered latency during therapy, some dilemmas will be illustrated. He was able to make good use of therapy but conscious and unconscious processes came into play to facilitate or resist the therapeutic aim of making experience conscious and thereby achieving integration. He placed prohibitions on the therapist which the therapist respected while also asserting an awareness of the motivations towards these. Through this means respect was given to his growing desire for autonomy without final surrender to the omnipotence of the world of paranoid-schizoid functioning. The child and the therapist were able to consent to a therapy which met the developmental potential and need at that point without indulging in the self-deceit of ‘cure’.

This book is one the New Library of Psychoanalysis series published in association with the Institute of Psycho-Analysis, London. It is an English, revised version of a book originally published in Italy in 1992 under a different title. There is a useful introduction by Elizabeth Bott Spillius, current general editor of the series and editor of the two volumes of Melanie Klein Today. Spillius helpfully sets Ferro's ideas in context for readers who may be unfamiliar with either Ferro's writings or the theoretical concepts he frequently refers to and draws upon. Spillius also comments on a number of themes connected with Ferro's ideas, and discusses some areas of controversy.

Ferro's book as a whole is concerned with the issue of how the analytic encounter between analyst and patient is conceived of and formulated, how the analyst stays open to emotional contact and meaning, the question of ‘hierarchy in [interpretative] codes and [theoretical] models’, and the related theme of how these determine the activity of interpretation. A central metaphor for Ferro is that of analyst and patient as a ‘group of two’, the point being that, as in any group, it is not always immediately clear what projective identifications belong to whom.

Inji Ralph

Inji Ralph

Inji Ralph   Trained as a child psychotherapist at the Anna Freud Centre where she is currently working on a part-time basis. She has worked in the NHS and taught on a number of AFC courses including the clinical training, the MSc in psychoanalytic developmental psychology and the short course on parent-infant mental health. She currently also works in private practice and has a special interest in parent-infant psychotherapy.
Sexual abuse, enactment, countertransference, foster carers, premature termination, imaginary twin,

This paper examines the development of a therapeutic relationship with a sexually abused latency girl who, in the course of her two years of four times weekly psychotherapy, was placed in two different foster-homes. It is argued that the child's re-enactment of the abuse in the consulting room allowed her to move from a seductive relationship with the therapist to one characterized by basic trust. This was paralleled by her development of a capacity to think and to tolerate affect states. The use of an imaginary twin by the child and the use of powerful countertransference feelings in the therapist are seen as the main therapeutic tools in the treatment. The premature termination of the treatment—due to the therapist's departure—enabled the child to articulate for the first time her feelings, in the transference, about the trauma and the traumatizing agent. The child's progressing moves in the therapy are also presented.

Editorial

Mary Walker and Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

We are pleased to present this first edition of 2001 in a new and larger format. We hope that readers will approve of the change which, as well as bringing the Journal into line with a more standard journal format, also gives us more space to publish papers, reviews and correspondence.

All the papers in this edition are concerned with challenging clinical situations and the demands they make on therapists to re-think their technique, theory and approach. This is not only a matter of adherence to a particular school of thought. These are critical life-and-death concerns: sometimes it is literally the patient's life that is at stake, at others it may be their psychic ‘aliveness’. It is, therefore, not surprising that discussion of these issues provokes strong feelings, as with the ‘Controversial Discussions’. However, it will be only through full and frank debate that our work will advance and in this spirit we have invited some senior members of the profession to write commentaries on Monica Lanyado's paper in response to the challenging issues she has raised. We hope that this debate might continue in the correspondence section so that the Journal can continue to develop as a forum for advancing our scientific knowledge to the benefit of all our patients and our profession.

This edition opens with Ann Horne's paper ‘Brief communications from the edge’ and is followed by Monica Lanyado's paper ‘The symbolism of the story of Lot and his wife’. Both Lanyado and Horne describe work with adolescents who are ‘on the edge’ and the struggle they had both to engage the patient and to remain in helpful therapeutic contact. Technical innovations are described which challenge a more orthodox psychoanalytic view of how certain communications by the patient might be handled: to what extent can these be contained within an interpretative stance or is some more concrete response needed? Does this kind of ‘demonstration’ need to precede interpretative work proper, taking account of the patient's stage of emotional development, or does it indeed constitute a form of interpretation? The thorny question of whether a distinction can be made between the therapist as a transference object or as a new, developmental object is highlighted. This issue is taken up in the commentaries on Lanyado's paper. The four commentaries by Gabrielle Crockatt, Miranda Davies, Viviane Green and Peter Wilson respectively provide a thought-provoking range of differing responses to the theoretical and technical questions raised by Lanyado.

Editorial

Paul Barrows and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

In producing the present edition we began with the aim of collecting together a number of papers that would reflect the international scope of the journal, in terms of both its readership and its authors. In the event we have also achieved a second unexpected but very welcome outcome, namely to produce an edition that honours the work of Frances Tustin.

The first four papers all pay tribute to the enduring influence of her work. Maiello's paper, of course, was the winner of the First International Frances Tustin Memorial Prize in 1997 - a memorial established by Judith and Theodore Mitrani in Los Angeles. Maiello draws on and extends the implications of Tustin's ideas about the importance of trauma in the aetiology of autism. Houzel, who worked closely with Tustin, develops another aspect of her thinking in his paper in which he seeks to redress the balance which he feels has over-emphasized the importance of Oedipal rivalry as against sibling rivalry. Fonseca and colleagues illustrate the degree of shared understanding that there can now be among analysts about autistic states and how Tustin's work with psychogenic autism may be extended to work with brain-damaged autistic children. Mori, in her paper, like Maiello, also emphasizes the importance of trauma as an aetiological factor in autism, and movingly shows how she was able to begin to make contact with her patient.

The papers are an impressive illustration of the breadth of Tustin's ideas. These have proved far-reaching in their implications, not only for our understanding of the genesis of autistic states, but also for our appreciation of the role played by autistic enclaves in more neurotic patients (see, for example, Mitrani, 2001). As these papers show, they have also reached far geographically: from South America to the opposite side of the world in Japan. Tustin would have been enormously heartened to see how her work has flourished in this way. She was of course, it should be added, an Honorary Member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists - and a regular contributor to this journal.

This book publishes the papers, principally by André Green and Daniel Stern, with other interventions which were given at a day conference on Psychoanalysis and Infant Observation in 1997. These are preceded by an introduction by Riccardo Steiner and an earlier exchange between André Green and Robert Wallerstein on psychoanalytic research.

I was present at this conference, and recall feeling how unreasonably hostile was the treatment meted out to Daniel Stern by André Green, and, in collusion with him at least, by some other participants. Stern was accused of being allied to the enemies of psychoanalysis. He said that he did not at all want to destroy psychoanalysis. ‘I feel that by contributing to a discourse that conceivably has indirect relevance, psychoanalysis will stay much healthier.’

A considerable extraneous burden of controversy overshadowed this debate. In the background lay a fierce argument about the role of ‘research’ in psychoanalysis, a strongly contested cause which has become something of a band-wagon in the IPA and in the British Psychoanalytical Society. Green and Stern became positioned as spokespersons respectively for the ‘non-scientific’ essence of psychoanalysis and for scientism, descriptions which in reality fit neither of them very well. There were also echoes in the debate of an earlier public debate on Stern's work in London, including a memorable exchange in which the apparently sunny natures of the Geneva babies he studies in his laboratories were compared with the more fractious Kleinian infants observed in London. In this book there is thus too much position taking, and too little receptive response (with some exceptions, such as Anne Alvarez's generous-spirited contribution) to what was actually said. The adversarial format of debate did not prove conducive to reflection.

To my mind, the only new work presented at the conference was that reported by Daniel Stern. One is inclined therefore to read the debate as a manifestation of how at this point new ideas from somewhere at least adjacent to psychoanalysis are being received in the psychoanalytic profession. Stern describes his observations of mother-baby interactions, over small segments of time, the way he constructed them, and the inferences he draws from them. What is initially most striking is his account of his methodological approach.

Monica Lanyado  

Transition and change: a response to commentaries on ‘The symbolism of the story of Lot and his wife’

My paper was written in the spirit of attempting to stimulate discussion, so I welcomed the Editors’ decision to invite comments from Gabrielle Crockatt, Miranda Davies, Viviane Green and Peter Wilson. Their ideas have indeed proved stimulating, so I am glad to have this opportunity to respond with what is in effect a ‘brain-storm’ to the points they have made. I intend to discuss these thoughts more fully in the future.

The therapist as a new developmental object and the present relationship

Viviane Green draws our attention to Fonagy's paper which concludes that the changes that took place in the analysis of a patient who seemed impervious to transference interpretations could be seen as being the result of the analyst becoming a new developmental object for the patient (Fonagy, 1999; Hurry, 1998).

Peter Wilson writes

Monica Lanyado's paper reminds me of a cartoon by Callahan about a psychoanalyst and his patient. The psychoanalyst is seated, facing away from the patient as is customary, nose in the air, in repose, absorbed. Meanwhile, behind him, his patient is on the floor - flattened, pinned beneath an upturned couch, in disarray, sprawling towards the psychoanalyst. The caption reads: ‘Basically, Mr. Wilson, what I seem to be hearing you say is, “Help”’.

The joke is on the psychoanalyst - the professional, out of tune, sublimely unaware, not in touch. And yet, of course, the joke exists in context; it sits within the well-established and valued tradition of psychoanalytic neutrality or detachment. It is important that the psychoanalyst keeps his distance, holds his breath, keeps time and space for thought and reflection. It matters too that he constrains his embrace to stay alert to the force and meaning of the entanglements of transference. The absurdity in the cartoon resides in the necessity of the (psychoanalytic) discipline.

And yet the patient is on the floor - in deep trouble, unable for the time being to deal with himself. It may be that the psychoanalyst's timely words will capture the moment, touch the underlying anxiety and help mobilize the patient to the upright state. It may well be too that the psychoanalyst's still composure provides sufficient containment - heightening, through resisting enactment, the potential for insight.

She is supervisor of psychotherapy, officially certified by the Japan Psychoanalytical Association.
Autistic state, affect attunement, self-object experience, dimensionality of mental function

In this paper, I describe the first part of a seven-year period of once weekly therapy with an autistic boy aged 4 at the start of treatment. By careful attunement to his affect and internal state, the therapist was able to engage him, allowing him eventually to come out of withdrawal. During this process, the self-object experiences between the patient and the therapist played a remarkable role. I was helped in my thinking by Tustin's (1981) view of the traumatized autistic child and by Meltzer's (1975) work regarding dimensionality in mental function. The patient was a child with cumulative psychic trauma arising from the mother-child relationship. At the start of therapy he was absent-minded and vacant. In the safe, protected therapeutic space, he was able to experience, perhaps for the first time, affective attunement with another. After a year of therapy, communication became possible when the therapist could contain the child's projective identification. He established a more robust skin-ego as he started to play out fantasies and stories symbolizing separation and reunion.

This paper reviews Frances Tustin's concept of the ‘autistic object’ and its development over the course of her writings. Clinical material from work with a 4-year-old boy is brought to suggest that the concept can usefully be extended to include such cultural artefacts as stories as well as the physical objects emphasized by Tustin. Generally speaking, psychoanalysis has focused far less on sibling rivalry than on its Oedipal counterpart. The author explores the reasons for this discrepancy from what is known of Freud's personal background as reported, inter alia, in his self-analysis. He reviews the theories that Jacques Lacan and Melanie Klein put forward as regards fantasies about sibling rivalry. Viviane Green Writes

When I was asked if I would consider doing a commentary on a paper the request finished with the remark that the paper was ‘a bit controversial’. This was sufficiently intriguing to arouse curiosity and produce a ‘yes’.

In the first section of the paper, Lanyado sets out to explain and elaborate on why the land beyond transference interpretations as a force for therapeutic change needed

37

addressing. In clearly setting out the reasons for looking at the therapeutic impact of the child psychotherapist as a new developmental figure, there was a sense that the writer had ‘to dare to bare’, in the face of a historical collective psychoanalytic superego murmuring ‘but this is not real analysis’. It was this tone, that the whole venture was somehow risky and about to meet with disapprobation, that was so intriguing to this particular reader who imagined that many child psychotherapists would be interested in the notion of the therapist as a new developmental figure and arriving at formulations similar to Lanyado's. Hurry's chapter ‘Psychoanalysis and developmental therapy’, in the book of the same title, argues cogently that there is no essential dichotomy between psychoanalysis and developmental help:

our understanding of developmental disturbances and of ways of treating them has been greatly enriched by findings from infant observational research, for the interactions that take place within the therapeutic developmental relationship are essentially similar to those that ordinarily take place between parents and the infant or child. (Hurry 1998: 38)

The therapist enters the child's developmental stream as both a transference and a new developmental object. If there is a therapeutic Zeitgeist then it is precisely the questions and preoccupations in Lanyado's paper that are at its centre. The paper is timely and to be welcomed. It furthers the possibility of thinking about the specific features that effect therapeutic change in a fresh way. It also pushes us to ask further questions.

David Trevatt  

This rather modestly titled study of research and clinical experience of borderline children is in fact a very important contribution, bringing together some widely varying views and theoretical ideas. The first part of the book, ‘Crossing The Borders’, takes the reader on a detailed tour of the research findings in the USA and the British-based psychoanalytical schools. There have been many attempts to identify and define borderline phenomena in different traditions, as well as different countries and continents. The aim in this book is to ‘synthesize’ some of the ideas from the schools of psychoanalysis and developmental psychology and to find common ground or a bridge between them to attempt a harmonized clinical approach.

In the first chapter Lubbe looks at the historical origins for diagnosing borderline psychotic disorder (BPD) in children. It is clear that this ‘in-between’ area of functioning, which may have neurotic and psychotic features, is not an easy syndrome to define and it raises many questions about what could and should be included in its symptomatology. Indeed, there are many theorists who disagree about the domain in which borderline children can be diagnostically placed.

Originally BPD in children was understood as emerging from the study of borderline adults. However the early psychoanalytical work with children formed the basis for defining the condition as clinically distinct in itself, and this served to inform the clinical work with adults. Borderline refers to the area between psychosis and neurosis where phenomena of both types may be present at any time. The patient within the borderline range may cross the border in either direction, rather than inhabiting one zone more permanently. These children do not fit in established categories. They are not autistic or schizophrenic and their problems are in part due to ‘specific developmental imbalances’ (p. 36). It is somewhat gratifying that psychotherapeutic treatment is evidently successful in helping many children with this disorder.

Christopher Bollas

Christopher Bollas

9 Rosslyn Mews

Christopher Bollas  

Darwin and Freud changed the way we think of life (and death), finding in the natural world a harsh lesson—destruction moves us—that challenges anyone to come up with a beneficent view of human reality. What stories can we tell one another about the good life after coming to this conclusion?

‘They both decreed, in different ways, the death of immortality’, writes Adam Phillips in Darwin's Worms. In erasing belief in our endlessness they introduced us to ‘transience’. Darwin found beauty in the ruthless exchange of the natural world; its variation was inspiring. Freud found through the death instinct the right amount of death in life; indeed, a life would inevitably be judged on how artfully anyone constructed his or her own death. Permanence was out, discontinuity was in: mourning the losses was the ordinary emotional fate of anyone.

Darwin wrote about worms at the beginning and at the end of his life. Phillips argues that in the worm Darwin found a kind of unsung hero, a soul that works the earth, ‘sustaining its fertility’. Suffering as he did from digestive problems throughout his life, interestingly Darwin finds in a lowly creature not only a superior digestive ability, but something like a ‘kind of faith’. Darwin had ‘been able to describe, through the worms, that the earth could look after itself’.

Darwin avoided anything like a direct critique of contemporary theology. ‘For Darwin the best way of writing about theology was to write about science.’ Darwin's works propose a new form of afterlife, i.e. ‘the life of the world that continues after one's own death’.

Amputation; trauma; loss; mourning; omnipotence.

This paper describes two years of psychotherapy with Michael, a 13-year-old boy who had undergone a recent emergency amputation of his leg and hip for bone cancer. The work follows Michael's struggle with the enormity of the loss, in the face of his, as well as the system's, use of denial. The amputation as an ‘attack’ on his physical and emotional autonomy strikes at his early adolescent development. The therapeutic process is aided by his capacity ‘to go back to the unhappiness’. The therapy develops from his initial shock, to despair and self-blame, as he struggles with a tendency — in the middle period of the therapy — to lose his mind as well as his leg in a retreat to withdrawal and mindlessness, or to mania. He struggles between an omnipotent, at times self-destructive, wish to ‘go it alone’, versus a capacity to feel sad and to value life. His capacity to think about the trauma and to find meaning emerges. The paper raises questions about whether some trauma can ever be fully assimilated, and whether, for Michael, the mourning process could lead to a reintegrated sense of self and of a ‘psychic intactness’, dependent on the survival of his good ‘internal couple’.

Hospital and ward-based child psychotherapy and its limitations are explored.

Letter to the Editors from Dr Nina Vasilyeva, St Petersburg

Internalizing psychoanalytic thinking

At the beginning of the century there were strong psychoanalytic traditions in Russian psychiatry. However, from the middle of the 1930s, psychoanalysis was buried in oblivion for many years in Russia. Pavlov's theory was the dominant theory of psychiatry and psychotherapy. On the psychotherapy stage there remained hypnotic suggestion, rational and explanatory therapies.

Psychology assumed the form of an academic science. For many decades Russian psychology existed within its own empire. Only rarely was there any real exchange of information with the West. Language and scientific-cultural barriers made it difficult for Eastern Europeans to access Western texts or to publish in the West. So, important figures in Russian psychology, such as Teplov, Lomov, Leontiev, Rubinshtein, Nebilytsin, Ananyev, Bernshtein, remained virtually unknown abroad (Foreman, 1997).

After the period of ‘perestroika’ in the 1980s the situation began to change rapidly. There arose a new openness to foreign contacts and information. It is difficult to count how many foreign psychotherapists and psychoanalysts have visited Russia over the past fifteen years. They have presented to Russian psychologists and psychiatrists almost all of the world's existing psychotherapy schools and stimulated the development of these in Russia. The independent education system, which began with workshops and seminars, gradually took the form of independent schools which are also psychotherapy centres.

Since the summer of 1996, the situation in psychoanalysis has begun to change. The President's Decree proclaimed the necessity to revive psychoanalysis in Russia. A committee was organized in Moscow. Active preparatory work started. Over time it became clear that new psychoanalytic developments in Russia were taking two differing paths. One was the state level, where committees are introducing their own requirements for the new profession. It is the way of large institutions and state medical centres. The major problem here seems to be the absence of any experience in psychoanalysis in the Russian medical profession. There are no trained psychoanalysts in the country. The danger therefore is that the whole process may take an artificial or amateurish form. At the same time there exist quite a few smaller groups of psychiatrists and psychologists who have chosen international standards for their training.

Brain development; neuroplasticity; early trauma; stress response.

The last decade has seen a vast increase in knowledge of how the human brain develops. It has been demonstrated that both the establishment of synaptic connections between neurones and the programming of neurochemical responses that have an effect on the whole body are dependent on experience. The most sensitive period for brain growth, the time of optimal plasticity, is over the first two or three years of life. If the baby's neurological development is threatened by abuse or neglect, which includes excessive attachment disruption, the damage may set its stamp on the rest of life.

Trauma; omnipotence; symbolic thinking; containment.

This paper describes intensive psychotherapy with a 3½-year-old boy who had come close to death at 10 days old, with urinary reflux and meningitis. The paper describes the way in which Jamie protected himself from unbearable terrors by being in identification with a builder. It tracks the way in which containment in the therapy allowed him to begin a process of experimenting with different identities through engaging in pretend play. The latter part of the paper looks at Jamie's subsequent development and examines the links between trauma and inconsistencies in his capacity for symbolic thought.

This clinical paper describes once weekly psychotherapy with two boys with traumatic histories. The way in which the trauma enters the consulting room and the relationship with the therapist is explored. Technical issues are discussed, particularly the understanding of the countertransference and its modulation in communication with the patient. The therapist's intense personal anxiety about failure and about management of the difficulties that arise is linked to the impact of trauma.

Prenatal auditory perception; sound-object; prenatal trauma; autism.

Through the clinical history of a little girl, this paper explores some possible traumatic prenatal experiences of children who have autistic features from birth. It establishes a tentative connection between the precocity of the onset of pathology and potentially traumatic prenatal situations such as threats of miscarriage or pathological mental states in the pregnant mother. It is suggested that a psycho-physical retreat from the auditory experience of the mother's voice, which normally stimulates foetal proto-mental activity and may lead to the development of a ‘sound-object’, might contribute to the later autistic child's isolation and non-mental clinging to tactile sensations.

Child abuse; mother-child relationship; mothers; parenting.

The paper describes the case of a girl of 8 weeks, referred by her mother because of ‘intolerable hysterical attacks’ triggering maternal impulses of abuse. Maternal perception of her infant was distorted to the extent that the mother was re-experiencing encounters with her own intrusive and traumatizing mother in the face of her screaming child. She also perceived the infant's motor impulses as physical attacks on herself and expressed intense anxieties about her daughter's future aggressive potential.

The infant was viewed by her mother as extraordinarily and dangerously greedy. Even neutral infantile vocalizations were perceived as manipulating and sadistic. She tried to ward off these anxieties by employing a rigid scheme of rules and obsessively controlling the father's and grandmother's interaction with the child. The mother feared being overwhelmed by the infant's needs if she were to yield to them in a flexible way.

The mother's background of early neglect and trauma is described, in the light of recent literature about the early intergenerational transmission of traumatic experiences, in order to demonstrate possible treatment modalities and the need to consider both protective and risk factors.

A Technique for Opening up a Psychic Space in Child Psychotherapy

Trevor Hartnup

28 Chemin de la Creuse Voie

Trevor Hartnup  

Concrete states of mind, deadening, hide and seek,

Working with concrete states of mind confronts the analyst with major countertransference problems: faced with the emptiness of the patient's psychic functioning, the analyst is threatened with the deadening of his own psychic capacities and the crumbling of the analytic process.

This paper examines two cases of children who presented in very different ways, one featuring deep-rooted depression and empty behaviour, the other featuring mastery and destructive omnipotence. It proposes a specific technique to enable the reconstruction of representational functioning through play. In the context of the transference/countertransference relationship and the analytic process, the introduction of a game of imaginary hide and seek, whose rules are defined and analysed, may represent an instrument of choice for opening up an undeveloped psychic space in these pathologies.

Gabriella Klein  

This book is made up of a series of eight lectures given in Sheffield by child psychotherapists, as part of the Tavistock model observational studies course. This particular course was attended by a wide range of professionals who were also able to attend individual lectures, and it was therefore adapted to meet their mixed needs.

This book has an excellent introductory chapter, written by the editors. It helpfully describes the salient issues to be elaborated in the lectures: Oedipal development and the capacity for thinking, which constitute the two central themes of the book, and which serve to link the chapters and give the whole an inner coherence. Each chapter was written by a different presenter and has a distinctive stylistic tone. Their approaches to their material are diverse, with varying degrees of emphasis on theory, observational material and clinical material. But the common themes, as described by the editors, and perhaps also the fact the writers were all Tavistock trained, ensure the book has a feeling of continuity. It is also evidence of the shared recognition of the centrality of these issues to a psychoanalytic understanding of personality development.

The editors explain some fundamental psychoanalytic concepts, perhaps as a way of introducing these to readers who are unfamiliar with them. The editors write, ‘The aim of the course…was to focus on ordinary development … development as a process…. The metaphor of a spiral best illustrates the juxtaposition of linear time with the circularity of the internal experience that we are attempting to capture and describe.’ While the external world of the developing personality is evident throughout the book to a lesser or greater degree, it is the focus on the developing internal world which repeatedly takes the reader back to considering Oedipal issues and the ability to think. Linking these with infantile parts of the developing personality and with the notion of the spiral helps to give the reader a sense of the necessary reworking of developmental tasks at different stages of development.
